Section 01The computational question behind a two-dimensional spectrum

A linear spectrum asks how a single optical coherence evolves. A third-order, two-dimensional electronic spectrum asks a more elaborate question: what happens when three ordered interactions with light prepare, transform, and read out coherences and populations? The result depends on two coherence intervals, a waiting interval, the side of the density operator on which each pulse acts, and transitions into the two-excitation manifold. Increasing the number of molecules therefore makes both the quantum-state problem and the sampling problem more expensive.

This paper extends the efficient propagation methods of the companion linear-spectroscopy paper to this third-order problem. Its distinctive ideas are sparse operations in each excitation manifold, rank-one forward–backward estimators, importance sampling of optical reinitializations, and batched calculation of branches associated with different pulse delays. Each idea addresses a different computational cost. None means that a spectrum can contain an arbitrarily large number of independently resolved points without additional work or memory.

These notes derive the optical response before discussing its numerical representation. We construct actual matrices, follow six selected pathways one operator multiplication at a time, derive an unbiased sampling distribution, and explain how trajectory branching changes the calculation. The embedded teaching program evaluates a small, finite-system Lindblad reference and tests the sampling algebra. It does not include the article's non-Markovian molecular bath, PLDM nuclear trajectories, or GPU implementation.

Primary source: J. Chem. Phys. 162, 074110 (2025), including the appendices contained in the supplied article. The published title is “2D non-linear spectra”; the website previously used a descriptive shortened title. Equation numbers on this page are tutorial numbers.

Section 02Spaces, units, and the meaning of the three times

We write Hamiltonians in energy units. The light–matter matrix element is vn=ℏgn, the cavity energy is Ec=ℏωc, and the molecular vertical excitation energy is ϵn. Spectral axes can be angular frequencies, energies, or wavenumbers, but the Fourier exponential must use matching units. For an energy axis it is exp⁡(iEt/ℏ), not exp⁡(iEt).

The ordered pulse delays are t1≥0, the first coherence interval; t2≥0, the waiting interval; and t3≥0, the detection interval. The absolute interaction times can be chosen as 0,t1,t1+t2, with detection at t1+t2+t3. The density operator during t2 need not be a population: off-diagonal coherences within one excitation manifold can also evolve during this interval.

The total Hilbert space is

H=HS⊗HB,HS=(⨂n=1Nspan{|gn⟩,|en⟩})⊗Hc.
(1)

A physical state ρ^SB is different from a response operator generated by a pulse sequence. The latter may have zero trace, be non-Hermitian, or carry a complex statistical weight. It is not generally legitimate to normalize it as though it were a physical density matrix.

Section 03The Hamiltonian and excitation-number conservation

The Holstein–Tavis–Cummings Hamiltonian has the form

H^=H^S⊗I^B+I^S⊗H^B+∑nn^n⊗B^n,
(2)
H^S=Eca^†a^+∑nϵnn^n+∑n(vnσ^n†a^+vn∗a^†σ^n),n^n=σ^n†σ^n.
(3)

The local operators obey σ^n2=0, whereas the cavity satisfies the oscillator ladder rule a^|q⟩=q|q−1⟩. The bath operators B^n are linear combinations of local harmonic coordinates. Independent baths can have identical statistics without being the same bath.

The rotating-wave Hamiltonian conserves N^exc=a^†a^+∑nn^n. Its field-free propagator is therefore block diagonal in excitation number. A molecular dipole changes excitation number by one; photon leakage decreases it. This structure determines which blocks an optical pathway can visit.

Source: Sec. II A. The treatment of complex couplings here is an explicit tutorial extension of the real-coupling notation.

Section 04Why third-order absorption needs the second manifold

Use |G⟩ for the molecular ground state with zero photons, |c⟩ for one photon, and |n⟩ for one molecular excitation. The three retained manifolds are

B0=(|G⟩),B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,…,|N⟩),B2=(|cc⟩,|c1⟩,…,|cN⟩,|12⟩,|13⟩,…).
(4)

Here |cn⟩ has one photon and one molecular excitation. A state |nm⟩ requires n≠m, because each molecule is two-level. Counting these states gives

d0=1,d1=N+1,d2=1+N+(N2),K=d0+d1+d2=N2+3N+62.
(5)

For N=1,2,5,25, the dimensions are K=5,8,23,353, respectively. In particular, d2=326 and K=353 for 25 two-level molecules in this complete cutoff. A different reported state count must correspond to a different retained subspace, convention, or typographical error; it should not replace this combinatorial construction without an explanation.

Two excitations are sufficient for the usual ground-state third-order GSB, SE, and ESA pathways under the rotating-wave approximation. They are not sufficient for arbitrary strong pulses, higher-order responses, or thermally populated high-excitation initial conditions.

Section 05A complete dimer Hamiltonian in eight states

For two molecules, order the full basis as

B=(|G⟩;|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩;|cc⟩,|c1⟩,|c2⟩,|12⟩).
(6)

At a fixed nuclear configuration, the Hamiltonian is diag(0,H^1,H^2), with

[H^1]=(Ecv1∗v2∗v1ϵ10v20ϵ2),
(7)
[H^2]=(2Ec2v1∗2v2∗02v1Ec+ϵ10v2∗2v20Ec+ϵ2v1∗0v2v1ϵ1+ϵ2).
(8)

The coupling from |cc⟩ to |c1⟩ has a 2 photon factor. The coupling from |c1⟩ to |12⟩ excites molecule 2 and has no such factor. These two operations should not be assigned the same matrix element merely because both increase the number of excited molecules by one.

The local bath-coupling projectors are especially simple:

[n^1]=diag(0;0,1,0;0,1,0,1),[n^2]=diag(0;0,0,1;0,0,1,1).
(9)

Each matrix is positive semidefinite. Transforming to polariton eigenstates changes its entries but not its eigenvalues or positivity. This is a useful check on sign conventions in transformed bath operators.

Section 06The molecular dipole as a rectangular block map

For a specified pulse polarization let dn be the projected transition-dipole matrix element. Define

μ^+=∑ndnσ^n†,μ^−=(μ^+)†,μ^=μ^++μ^−.
(10)

The molecular dipole does not create a cavity photon directly. In the dimer basis, its nonzero raising blocks are

[μ^+]10=(0d1d2),[μ^+]21=(000d100d2000d2d1).
(11)

Thus μ^+|c⟩=d1|c1⟩+d2|c2⟩, while μ^+|1⟩=d2|12⟩. A putative |11⟩ term must vanish. The complete eight-state matrix is

[μ^+]=(000[μ^+]10000[μ^+]210)B0⊕B1⊕B2.
(12)

A model driven through the cavity instead would use an optical operator proportional to a^+a^†. That is a different experimental coupling and changes transition strengths. It should not be substituted silently for molecular excitation.

Section 07Deriving the causal third-order response

Take a real applied field E(t) and the interaction V^(t)=−E(t)μ^. In the interaction picture with respect to the field-free Hamiltonian,

dρ^Idt=iℏE(t)[μ^I(t),ρ^I(t)].
(13)

Integrating once and substituting the integral equation into itself generates a time-ordered perturbation series. At third order,

ρ^I(3)(t)=(iℏ)3∫−∞tds3∫−∞s3ds2∫−∞s2ds1E(s3)E(s2)E(s1)×[μ^I(s3),[μ^I(s2),[μ^I(s1),ρ^eq]]].
(14)

The detected polarization is P(3)(t)=Tr(μ^I(t)ρ^I(3)(t)). Returning to a field-free propagation notation gives the impulse-response kernel

R(3)(t3,t2,t1)=(iℏ)3Tr[μ^G^(t3)μ^×G^(t2)μ^×G^(t1)μ^×ρ^eq],
(15)

where μ^×O^=[μ^,O^]. The propagator acts on an operator, not just on a ket. For exact non-Markovian dynamics, G^ here is the full system–bath propagator, or an equivalent enlarged-space representation retaining the relevant memory. A reduced-system map inferred from a factorized initial condition cannot simply be restarted after every pulse.

The factor i3=−i and the minus signs from right actions are bookkeeping, but they matter. Writing them explicitly at the beginning prevents a sign error from being “corrected” later by flipping a plotted spectrum.

Section 08Left and right multiplication as Liouville-space matrices

Use column vectorization: |O^⟩⟩ stacks the columns of O^. In the operator basis (|a⟩⟨b|),

|A^O^B^⟩⟩=(B^T⊗A^)|O^⟩⟩.
(16)

Consequently the matrices for left multiplication, right multiplication, and a commutator are

[L^μ]=I^⊗μ^,[R^μ]=μ^T⊗I^,[μ^×]=I^⊗μ^−μ^T⊗I^.
(17)

The transpose is not a Hermitian conjugate. It arises from column stacking. For unitary field-free motion, the generator is

[K^H]=−iℏ(I^⊗H^−H^T⊗I^).
(18)

For the eight-state dimer this matrix is 64×64. It is small enough for a reference calculation but grows as the square of the Hilbert-space dimension. The article's trajectory method avoids propagating a dense Liouville vector for every sampled bath configuration.

Section 09What a pulse does to a dyad

Let O^=|f⟩⟨b|. Left and right actions are

μ^+O^=(μ^+|f⟩)⟨b|,O^μ^−=|f⟩(⟨b|μ^−).
(19)

If the backward state is stored as a ket |b⟩, the second action changes it to μ^+|b⟩, because (⟨b|μ^−)†=μ^+|b⟩. If the backward object is stored directly as row coefficients, it instead multiplies μ^− from the right. Mixing these storage conventions produces conjugation errors.

For instance,

ρ^Gμ^−=∑eμeG∗|G⟩⟨e|,μ^+ρ^G=∑eμeG|e⟩⟨G|,ρ^G=|G⟩⟨G|.
(20)

Here |e⟩ labels a state in the first manifold, not necessarily a local molecular excitation. The two operators are conjugate optical coherences. The first belongs to the rephasing family and the second to the nonrephasing family for the convention used below.

Section 10Selecting the six rotating-wave pathways

A product of three commutators contains eight algebraic terms before optical-frequency and phase-matching selection. The familiar six GSB/SE/ESA pathways are not a claim that the unselected commutator has six terms. They are the relevant selected pathways and their conjugate structure for a ground-state, third-order experiment.

Define L±O^=μ^±O^ and R±O^=O^μ^±. Every pulse is followed by the propagation for that interval. Suppressing overall optical constants, the following table specifies our complete convention:

Family Contribution First action Second action Third action Relative sign
Rephasing GSB R− R+ L+ +
Rephasing SE R− L+ R+ +
Rephasing ESA R− L+ L+ −
Nonrephasing GSB L+ L− L+ +
Nonrephasing SE L+ R− R+ +
Nonrephasing ESA L+ R− L+ −

Every final operator is detected with Tr(μ^−O^). The listed relative signs absorb a common global phase so that GSB and SE have the same sign and ESA the opposite sign. The next sections verify this assignment by direct multiplication.

Source: Sec. II B and Fig. 6. The left/right table is an explicit tutorial reconstruction with a stated global-phase convention.

Section 11Ground-state bleach, multiplied out

Consider a real transition dipole d and one first-manifold eigenstate |e⟩. Temporarily ignore the bath and loss. The rephasing GSB sequence follows

|G⟩⟨G|→R−d|G⟩⟨e|→R+d2|G⟩⟨G|→L+d3|e⟩⟨G|.
(21)

The field-free phase of a dyad is

G^(t)|a⟩⟨b|=e−i(Ea−Eb)t/ℏ|a⟩⟨b|.
(22)

Thus the detected GSB contribution is proportional to

SR,GSB=d4e+iωeGt1e−iωeGt3,ωeG=(Ee−EG)/ℏ.
(23)

There is no excited-state phase during t2 in this simple isolated-state example because the operator is back in the ground block. This does not imply that a ground-state-bath wavepacket or a bath-conditioned GSB branch is stationary in a general molecular calculation. The bath history produced during t1 must still be treated correctly.

For nonrephasing GSB, the first coherence is |e⟩⟨G|, and the first phase is instead e−iωeGt1. That sign is the origin of the opposite first-axis Fourier transform.

Section 12Stimulated emission and waiting-time coherence

For rephasing SE, choose first-manifold states |e⟩ and |e′⟩. The operator sequence is

|G⟩⟨G|→R−|G⟩⟨e|→L+|e′⟩⟨e|→R+|e′⟩⟨G|.
(24)

Its phase is

SR,SEe′e∝e+iωeGt1e−i(Ee′−Ee)t2/ℏe−iωe′Gt3.
(25)

When e′=e, the middle operator is a population. When e′≠e, it is a coherence within the first manifold. Taking e′=+ and e=− produces beating at the upper–lower polariton energy splitting. This is why a two-dimensional cross peak can oscillate during the interval often called “population time.”

Population transfer, cavity loss, and dephasing change the amplitude and may generate additional contributions. Therefore a cross-peak intensity trace need not be a single damped cosine. A fitting model must account for offsets, overlapping pathways, and the chosen detection window.

Section 13Excited-state absorption and its opposite sign

The rephasing ESA sequence has the same first two interactions as SE, but the third pulse raises the ket into the second manifold:

|G⟩⟨G|→R−|G⟩⟨e|→L+|e′⟩⟨e|→L+|f⟩⟨e|,|f⟩∈H2.
(26)

Detection connects |f⟩ back to |e⟩. The resulting phase is

SR,ESAfe′e∝−e+iωeGt1e−i(Ee′−Ee)t2/ℏe−i(Ef−Ee)t3/ℏ.
(27)

The detection frequency is a first-to-second-manifold transition, not a ground-to-first-manifold transition. The negative relative sign follows because this selected sequence has a different number of right actions in the nested commutator. It is not an empirical convention chosen to make a plot look derivative-like.

A harmonic bosonic model may have cancellations between SE/GSB and ESA. A finite ensemble of two-level emitters has saturation and an anharmonic excitation ladder, so those cancellations are incomplete. Omitting ESA changes both the magnitude and shape of the total nonlinear signal.

Section 14An explicit ladder calculation and the large-ensemble limit

For identical emitters, equal real coupling v, and zero detuning, define the symmetric two-excitation states |cc⟩, |cB⟩=N−1/2∑n|cn⟩, and |BB⟩=(N2)−1/2∑n<m|nm⟩. For N≥2,

[H^2](cc,cB,BB)=2ϵI^+(02Nv02Nv02(N−1)v02(N−1)v0).
(28)

The eigenvalues are

E2,0=2ϵ,E2,±=2ϵ±v4N−2,E1,±=ϵ±vN.
(29)

The difference between the upper-branch ESA transition and the upper fundamental is

δEanh=(E2,+−E1,+)−E1,+=v4N−2−2vN.
(30)

At fixed collective coupling V=Nv, expanding 1−x=1−x/2+O(x2) gives

δEanh=2V(1−12N−1)=−V2N+O(N−2).
(31)

This is a precise way in which the bright ladder becomes more harmonic as the ensemble grows. It does not establish that the complete nonlinear signal scales only through this one transition: dipole strengths, dark states, disorder, and bath dynamics also matter. For N=1, |BB⟩ does not exist; use the two-state Jaynes–Cummings second manifold instead.

Section 15Rephasing, nonrephasing, and an absorptive convention

In the convention above, Fourier-transform the selected signals as

S~R(ω3,t2,ω1)=∫0∞dt3∫0∞dt1e+iω3t3−iω1t1SR(t3,t2,t1),
(32)
S~NR(ω3,t2,ω1)=∫0∞dt3∫0∞dt1e+iω3t3+iω1t1SNR(t3,t2,t1).
(33)

Then define the tutorial's absorptive signal by

Sabs=Re(S~R+S~NR).
(34)

The article writes its response with a different retained overall phase and takes a negative imaginary part. There is no contradiction when R=−iS: −ImR=ReS. What would be incorrect is to take the negative imaginary part of our phase-stripped S without restoring the corresponding factor.

For energy axes, replace ωjtj by Ejtj/ℏ. For the numerical integral, include Δt1Δt3, endpoint weights, and any chosen damping window. The spectrum is not simply the absolute square of a two-dimensional Fourier transform.

Section 16Why two-dimensional echoes distinguish disorder from memory

For static Gaussian energy disorder δϵ with variance σ2, a rephasing single-transition signal accumulates the random phase δϵ(t1−t3)/ℏ. The Gaussian characteristic function gives

⟨eiδϵ(t1−t3)/ℏ⟩=exp⁡[−σ2(t1−t3)22ℏ2].
(35)

For the nonrephasing family,

⟨e−iδϵ(t1+t3)/ℏ⟩=exp⁡[−σ2(t1+t3)22ℏ2].
(36)

The first expression can refocus near t3=t1; the second cannot for positive delays. Dynamic frequency fluctuations spoil perfect refocusing according to their correlation function. This elementary calculation explains why diagonal elongation and spectral diffusion contain information that is lost in a one-dimensional linewidth.

It does not imply that every polariton lineshape can be described by one Gaussian random frequency. Multiple eigenstates, ESA overlap, population transfer, and spatially local baths make the full problem richer.

Section 17Photon loss acts between and within excitation blocks

A Markovian photon-loss channel with population rate κ contributes

D^aO^=κ(a^O^a^†−12{a^†a^,O^}).
(37)

For the eight-state dimer,

a^=|G⟩⟨c|+2|c⟩⟨cc|+|1⟩⟨c1|+|2⟩⟨c2|.
(38)

The recycling term moves a block O^qr into O^q−1,r−1. In particular, an ESA coherence in the (2,1) block can feed a (1,0) optical coherence. Replacing the full dissipator by an imaginary cavity energy retains the anticommutator term but loses this feed-down.

In column-vectorized form,

[D^a]=κ[a^∗⊗a^−12I^⊗a^†a^−12(a^†a^)T⊗I^].
(39)

There is an additional modeling distinction: one channel a^ is not generally equivalent to separate channels for each transition appearing in a^. Cross terms in a^O^a^† transfer some coherences that independently resolved channels do not. The 2023 companion Deep Dive derives this distinction explicitly. The teaching reference here specifies a single collective cavity jump; it is not a silent reproduction of every loss-channel choice in a trajectory implementation.

Section 18A forward–backward trajectory is not a wavefunction population

The PLDM construction represents reduced operators through an ensemble of forward and backward amplitudes correlated with nuclear trajectories. Schematically,

ρ^S(t)≈Eξ[Wξ(t)|fξ(t)⟩⟨bξ(t)|].
(40)

The expectation is over the initial thermal nuclear variables, mapping variables or focused states, and any stochastic events. A single dyad may not be Hermitian or positive. Its complex weight is part of the estimator, not a probability to discard.

At a prescribed real nuclear configuration,

iℏd|f⟩dt=H^(R)|f⟩,−iℏd⟨b|dt=⟨b|H^(R).
(41)

Equivalently, both stored kets |f⟩ and |b⟩ obey the usual forward Schrödinger equation, with conjugation supplied when forming the bra. Directly stored backward row amplitudes obey the opposite-sign equation. The article's notation for backward mapping coefficients should be interpreted with this distinction in mind.

The physical approximation enters when nuclear forward–backward path differences are partially linearized. A shared nuclear path retains more structure than assigning all response intervals to an arbitrary fixed bath trace, but it is still not the exact quantum bath evolution in general.

Section 19How partial linearization generates a nuclear force

Introduce forward and backward nuclear paths and their mean and difference variables,

|R¯⟩=|RF⟩+|RB⟩2,|Z⟩=|RF⟩−|RB⟩.
(42)

For a smooth potential, the path-action difference is expanded in |Z⟩. Keeping only terms linear in this difference lets its path integral impose a classical-like equation for |R¯⟩. The electronic forward and backward amplitudes remain distinct. In a common mapping convention, ca=(xa+ipa)/2, with a separately propagated backward set.

For the diagonal local bath coupling, the force has the structure

R˙nα=Pnα/mnα,P˙nα=−mnαωnα2Rnα−cnαFnF+FnB2,
(43)

where FnF and FnB are the forward and backward mapping population functions appropriate to the chosen mapping normalization. For normalized ket demonstrations they reduce to ⟨f|n^n|f⟩ and ⟨b|n^n|b⟩, respectively. The precise mapping zero-point convention must be kept consistent with the estimator and focusing measure.

A pulse changes which electronic state the branch carries, so it changes the subsequent force. It does not justify drawing an unrelated thermal bath at that pulse. Such a redraw would erase response memory accumulated in the previous interval.

Section 20Sparse Hamiltonian and dipole actions

Writing a dense matrix is useful for understanding the basis, but production propagation need not store it. In the first manifold,

(H^1|f⟩)c=Ecfc+∑nvn∗fn,(H^1|f⟩)n=ϵnfn+vnfc.
(44)

This requires O(N) arithmetic. In the second manifold,

(H^2f)cc=2Ecfcc+2∑nvn∗fcn,(H^2f)cn=(Ec+ϵn)fcn+2vnfcc+∑m≠nvm∗fnm,(H^2f)nm=(ϵn+ϵm)fnm+vmfcn+vnfcm.
(45)

The total work is O(N2), proportional to the number of stored second-manifold amplitudes. Pair labels are unordered: store fnm once for n<m. A sum over partners must retrieve that same stored variable rather than inventing independent fnm and fmn.

The dipole action has an equally sparse structure. For example,

(μ^+f)cn=dnfc,(μ^+f)nm=dnfm+dmfn.
(46)

Sparse actions can therefore be used inside each polynomial propagator, on either trajectory branch, and at each optical interaction. This is the part of the algorithm that removes dense K×K algebra.

Source: Sec. III A and the companion linear-spectroscopy derivation.

Section 21Why reading an observable need not form a density matrix

For a rank-one operator,

Tr(A^|f⟩⟨b|)=⟨b|A^|f⟩.
(47)

To verify this, insert a complete basis:

∑j⟨j|A^|f⟩⟨b|j⟩=⟨b|(∑j|j⟩⟨j|)A^|f⟩.
(48)

Compute |y⟩=A^|f⟩ using a sparse operator action, then take one inner product. For a diagonal or sparse dipole map, this costs O(K) rather than first building all K2 products in |f⟩⟨b|. There is no approximation in this identity.

The same logic explains why a propagation expressed in terms of two kets can be much cheaper than an explicit dense density matrix. It does not remove the statistical variance of the average over many such dyads.

Section 22Deriving unbiased matrix-element importance sampling

Suppose a pulse transforms a branch into a matrix M^, expanded in the chosen ordered system basis:

M^=∑ijMij|i⟩⟨j|.
(49)

Select one pair (I,J) with any positive probability pij on every nonzero matrix element, and propagate the random operator

M^samp=MIJpIJ|I⟩⟨J|.
(50)

Its mean is exactly M^, because

E[M^samp]=∑ijpijMijpij|i⟩⟨j|=M^.
(51)

The weight is generally complex. It carries both magnitude and phase. Sampling a matrix element and then discarding its phase would produce a different operator; normalizing every sampled matrix to unit trace would usually be even worse, since off-diagonal basis dyads have zero trace.

The unbiasedness statement concerns this algebraic decomposition. Combining it with approximate PLDM propagation yields an unbiased sampling of that approximate estimator, not exact quantum dynamics.

Section 23Rank one reduces joint sampling to two one-dimensional draws

For M^=|u⟩⟨v|, Mij=uivj∗. Define

Su=∑i|ui|,Sv=∑j|vj|,pij=|Mij|∑ab|Mab|=|ui|Su|vj|Sv.
(52)

The normalization factorizes because ∑ij|ui||vj|=SuSv. Therefore draw I from pi=|ui|/Su and J independently from qj=|vj|/Sv. The sampled weight is

WIJ=SuSvuI|uI|vJ∗|vJ|,M^samp=WIJ|I⟩⟨J|.
(53)

Constructing the two distributions costs O(K); constructing a joint K2-element probability array is unnecessary. Entries with zero amplitude have zero probability and are never divided by. When either sum is zero, the complete branch is zero and can be terminated.

This uses absolute amplitudes, not Born probabilities |ui|2. Squared-amplitude sampling can still be made unbiased with the correct weight, but it is a different distribution and can have very poor variance for small amplitudes.

Source: Sec. III B, importance sampling. The explicit probability construction and validation below are included to make the sampling implementable without ambiguous cumulative-index notation.

Section 24A complex three-by-two example

Choose |u⟩=(1,i,−1/2)T and |v⟩=(2,−i)T. Then

[M^]=(2i2i−1−1−i/2),Su=5/2,Sv=3.
(54)

The row probabilities are (2/5,2/5,1/5), and the column probabilities are (2/3,1/3). For the second row and second column,

p22=2513=215,W22=−152,p22W22=−1=M22.
(55)

For the first row and second column, the weight is 15i/2, which contributes i after multiplication by its selection probability. An implementation that stores only real signs fails this example immediately.

The companion script tests the expectation by exact summation over all possible selections and then demonstrates convergence with seeded Monte Carlo samples. Exact enumeration should pass to machine precision; a Monte Carlo estimate is expected to fluctuate.

Section 25Cumulative distributions without correlated-index mistakes

Let Pi=∑a≤ipa and Qj=∑b≤jqb. Draw independent uniform random numbers r,s∈[0,1), then choose the first indices satisfying PI>r and QJ>s. This realizes pij=piqj.

Using the same uniform number independently in both marginal CDFs generally correlates the indices and does not produce the product distribution. A correct one-random-number implementation is possible, but it must use the residual position inside the selected row interval:

I=min{i:Pi>r},s=r−PI−1pI,J=min{j:Qj>s}.
(56)

Conditional on the selected row, s is uniform on [0,1), so the joint probability is correct. A formula involving products of cumulative row and column sums must not be interpreted as an ordinary flattened CDF unless the actual ordering and interval lengths have been derived.

For practical code, two independent draws are easier to inspect. Set the final cumulative entry to exactly one to avoid floating-point roundoff at the upper end, and use a seeded generator for reproducible debugging.

Section 26Why the absolute-value distribution is natural

For an estimator made of basis dyads, the Frobenius second moment is

E∥M^samp∥F2=∑ij|Mij|2pij.
(57)

Minimize this expression subject to ∑ijpij=1. A Lagrange multiplier η gives

−|Mij|2pij2+η=0⟹pij∝|Mij|.
(58)

This minimizes the instantaneous Frobenius second moment of this particular decomposition. It does not necessarily minimize the variance of a final observable after a long nonlinear trajectory, because the propagated response to different starting dyads can differ greatly. Observable-aware sampling or correlated sampling can improve a complete calculation, but must preserve the proper weights.

The statistical error of independent samples normally decreases as the inverse square root of their number when the variance is finite. Replacing a quadratic probability table by two linear tables improves per-sample cost; it does not automatically reduce the number of trajectories needed for convergence.

Section 27Applying sampling successively at optical interactions

A branch begins with thermal nuclear variables and a focused electronic dyad. An optical action produces a new rank-one dyad because left or right multiplication affects only one vector. Reexpressing that dyad as a sampled basis dyad updates a complex weight and selects the states that seed the next interval.

If a conditional estimator is unbiased for each incoming branch, the law of iterated expectation preserves unbiasedness through a sequence of such reinitializations:

E[E(M^j+1samp∣M^j,ξj)]=E[M^j+1].
(59)

Here ξj denotes the carried nuclear and stochastic history. The condition “given the history” is essential. Averaging the electronic state first and attaching a fresh bath afterward does not generally commute with nonlinear nuclear force propagation.

A practical implementation records the cumulative complex weight, the forward and backward focused labels, the nuclear coordinates and momenta, the absolute branch time, and any stochastic-loss bookkeeping. Zero branches can be dropped. Very small selection probabilities require variance monitoring rather than arbitrary removal.

Section 28Propagation with Chebyshev polynomials

For each short nuclear step, suppose the Hermitian quantum Hamiltonian has a safe spectral enclosure [Emin,Emax]. Define a=(Emax−Emin)/2, b=(Emax+Emin)/2, and H^′=(H^−bI^)/a. Then

e−iH^Δt/ℏ|f⟩=e−ibΔt/ℏ[J0(z)|f⟩+2∑m=1∞(−i)mJm(z)Tm(H^′)|f⟩],z=aΔt/ℏ.
(60)

The recurrence uses only Hamiltonian–vector products:

|q0⟩=|f⟩,|q1⟩=H^′|f⟩,|qm+1⟩=2H^′|qm⟩−|qm−1⟩.
(61)

This is where the sparse manifold operations enter. Apply the corresponding conjugate evolution to the stored backward row, or the ordinary ket evolution to the stored backward ket. Keep all scalar phase factors consistently across manifolds; optical response depends on relative phases between different excitation sectors.

The truncation order depends on z and the target error. A four-term approximation that works for one short timestep and one spectral width is not a universal propagator. Nuclear timestepping and polynomial truncation are separate convergence parameters.

Section 29Branching over pulse delays

A direct implementation loops over every (t1,t2), starts an associated trajectory branch, and samples many t3 values. Much work is repeated if identical early histories are propagated independently. A branching implementation instead saves or copies the state at an optical interaction, applies the appropriate pulse, and carries the resulting family of branches together.

For a batch of B branches, collect the forward amplitudes into a matrix whose columns are kets:

F^=(|f1⟩,|f2⟩,…,|fB⟩),[F^]∈CK×B.
(62)

Each column may see different nuclear coordinates, so the diagonal molecular energies can be branch-dependent. The light–matter connectivity is shared. Elementwise diagonal operations, reductions, pair-index operations, and batched contractions can be vectorized without changing the physical meaning of the branches.

A state copied at a pulse time must include its bath variables and estimator weight, not only its electronic amplitudes. Otherwise the branches share an incorrect history. GPU batching is therefore a change in data organization, not permission to disregard causal propagation.

Section 30Interpreting the advertised cost reduction

The article reports a dramatic reduction from dense state operations and nested time-loop evaluation, with a compact O(K)O(T0) description for its optimized, vectorized setup. It is important to identify what is being timed. Constant observed wall time over a tested range of a parallelized dimension is not constant total arithmetic work for arbitrarily large delay grids.

A fully resolved map at one waiting time has T1T3 complex samples. Saving it requires at least

Mmap=16T1T3 bytes
(63)

for complex128 data, before keeping separate pathways or multiple waiting times. A batch of forward and backward states alone requires

Melectronic=32KB bytes.
(64)

Nuclear positions, momenta, forces, temporary polynomial vectors, random-number states, and output accumulators add to this. The branch batch can be tiled when it does not fit device memory. Tiling preserves the calculation but changes the wall-time scaling as hardware capacity is exceeded.

The durable algorithmic conclusions are that sparse operations remove unnecessary dense algebra, rank-one sampling removes a quadratic joint probability table, and batching exploits parallelism. A reproducible benchmark should specify state dimensions, timestep, trajectory count, precision, number of devices, delay-grid size, and whether transfers and allocations were timed.

Source: Figs. 1–2 and Sec. III C. The arithmetic-versus-wall-time distinction and memory formulas are tutorial analysis, not an additional claim of measured performance.

Section 31Understanding the article's numerical spectra

The article compares several ensemble sizes and resolves the rephasing, nonrephasing, and summed absorptive signals. The reported ensemble comparison includes N=1,2,5,25. It demonstrates how the excitation ladder, collective splitting, bath-induced broadening, and ESA overlap alter the map; it is not merely a plot of two linear polariton resonances copied onto two axes.

In the ensemble comparison, the waiting time is fixed at zero and the propagation window is increased for the larger systems. That matters: narrower features require a longer coherent time window to resolve. Comparing peak widths on unequal windows without accounting for Fourier resolution would confuse numerical and physical narrowing.

For the five-molecule system, the paper separately examines GSB, SE, and ESA during waiting-time evolution with cavity loss. Tracking each signed component explains cancellations and identifies whether an emerging peak is inherited from a ground-state pathway, an excited-state coherence, an ESA transition, or a loss-enabled route.

Source figures What to examine What not to infer automatically
Figs. 1–2 State-operation and batched timing behavior Unlimited constant-cost time grids
Figs. 3–5 Ensemble-size changes in signed 2D lineshapes That every peak is a one-excitation energy
Fig. 6 Which side each optical interaction acts on That the full commutator has only six terms
Figs. 7–8 Cancellation and waiting-time changes by pathway That total cross-peak intensity equals one density element
Fig. 9 and appendix Different bright-state assignments within a pathway That every cross peak requires direct dark-state optical strength

Source: Sec. IV, ensemble spectra, and pathway-resolved results. This tutorial does not digitize or claim to reproduce those figures.

Section 32A cost-and-ladder calculator

The calculator evaluates exact state counts for the complete cutoff, a uniform resonant bright ladder, and simple storage estimates. The ensemble size does not control an assumed bath trajectory count. The spectral-grid inputs describe output storage only; they are not a timing prediction.

For the default five-molecule example, the single-manifold dimension is 6, the second-manifold dimension is 16, and the total is 23. With V=50 meV, E2,+−2ϵ=504−2/5≈94.868 meV. The upper-branch anharmonic shift is approximately −5.132 meV. This shift is a bright-ladder result without molecular bath dressing.

Section 33The finite-matrix reference and its validation

The embedded Python program builds the complete low-excitation basis from photon occupation and molecular bit strings. It constructs the Hamiltonian and molecular dipole independently of hand-written block formulas, then evaluates the six pathways with a finite-system Lindblad propagator. It also tests the rank-one sampling estimator on complex vectors.

python collective_2des_teaching.py --test
python collective_2des_teaching.py --demo --output collective_2des_demo.csv

The default demo is deliberately small. It reports a synthetic spectrum in a stated rotating frame with a collective photon-loss channel and optional detection-window damping. It omits the local molecular bath and PLDM nuclear dynamics. Its purpose is to check signs, transitions, excitation cutoffs, and numerical assembly—not to stand in for the published collective-bath simulation.

A sensible validation order is: check operator Hermiticity and commutators; compare sparse and dense actions; verify the pulse table with dyads; verify trace preservation for physical initial states; verify stochastic reinitialization by exact enumeration; compare a zero-bath response with direct matrices; then converge bath discretization, nuclear timesteps, polynomial order, trajectories, and delay windows in the production method.

Section 34Twelve worked checks

1. Count every state for three molecules.
There is one ground state, four states with one excitation, and 1+3+3=7 states with two excitations. Thus K=12. The three double-molecular states are |12⟩,|13⟩,|23⟩; none has two excitations on the same molecule. Adding a fictitious |11⟩ changes both the count and the nonlinear response.
2. Derive a dipole matrix element with a photon spectator.
Apply d1σ^1†+d2σ^2† to |g1g2;1⟩. The result is d1|e1g2;1⟩+d2|g1e2;1⟩. Hence ⟨c1|μ^+|c⟩=d1. There is no 2, because this operation does not change photon number.
3. Verify the sign of the first rephasing phase.
The first operator is |G⟩⟨e|. Its energy difference is EG−Ee=−ℏωeG, so evolution multiplies it by e+iωeGt1. The first-axis transform must therefore contain e−iω1t1 to place its resonance on the positive ω1 axis.
4. Identify what evolves during an off-diagonal SE waiting interval.
The second interaction can produce |+⟩⟨−|. Under the field-free Hamiltonian this acquires e−i(E+−E−)t2/ℏ. It is not a population, despite the conventional name “population time.” A fit to its ideal real signal has an angular frequency (E+−E−)/ℏ.
5. Locate an ESA peak in a resonant monomer.
For one emitter, E1,+=ϵ+v and E2,+=2ϵ+2v. The associated ESA detection energy is E2,+−E1,+=ϵ+(2−1)v, not ϵ+v. The difference from the upper fundamental is (2−2)v.
6. Check the two-manifold bright coupling for N = 2.
The matrix element between |cc⟩ and |cB⟩=(|c1⟩+|c2⟩)/2 is (2v+2v)/2=2v. The element between |cB⟩ and |12⟩ is (v+v)/2=2v. The upper bright shift is (2v)2+(2v)2=6v.
7. Reconstruct the negative matrix element in the complex sampling example.
The second-row/second-column probability is 2/15, and its weight is −15/2. Their product is −1. Replacing the phase with +1 would reconstruct +1 and fail even before propagation. The normalization SuSv is just as necessary as the phase.
8. Show why using the same uniform number for both marginals fails.
Take both marginal probabilities to be (1/2,1/2). Using the same random number gives only pairs (1,1) and (2,2), each with probability 1/2. The required product distribution gives all four pairs probability 1/4. Independent draws, or the residual-within-row construction, recover the correct distribution.
9. Compute output memory for a 512 × 512 map.
One complex128 map uses 16×5122=4,194,304 bytes, or 4 MiB. Six separately stored pathway maps use 24 MiB at one waiting time. Keeping 100 waiting times multiplies this again by 100. GPU parallelism does not erase these output dimensions.
10. Check a recycling term that a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian misses.
For O^=|cc⟩⟨c|, one has a^|cc⟩=2|c⟩ and ⟨c|a^†=⟨G|. Therefore κa^O^a^†=2κ|c⟩⟨G|. It creates a first-manifold optical coherence from a second-to-first-manifold response operator.
11. Convert between real-part and negative-imaginary-part conventions.
Write S=x+iy. Then −iS=y−ix, and −Im(−iS)=x=ReS. An overall phase convention is harmless when propagated consistently through the definition of the detected quantity. Applying the two projections to the same unmodified complex signal is not equivalent.
12. Separate exact identities from dynamical approximations.
The excitation count, sparse matrix action, dyad trace identity, and importance-sampling expectation are exact algebraic statements. A finite polynomial propagator has a numerical truncation error. Partial nuclear-path linearization is a dynamical approximation. Markovian cavity loss is a bath-model assumption. Agreement of the sampling test alone cannot validate any of the latter choices.

Section 35Connecting this method to the other papers

The 2025 linear-spectra notes derive the matrix-free Hamiltonian and polynomial propagator in more numerical detail. The 2023 notes develop the foundational response and stochastic-loss issues with explicit monomer and dimer examples. The PNAS notes focus on extracting polariton coherence and spectral-diffusion information from the resulting signal.

The methods form a sequence, but their roles should remain distinct: efficient propagation makes trajectories affordable; correct response bookkeeping makes the spectrum meaningful; convergence and a justified model determine whether its physical interpretation is reliable.
